html:
The Mali Empire was a West African empire of the Mandinka people on the upper Niger, founded about 1235 by Sundiata Keita. At its height in the 1300s it was the largest state in West Africa, reaching from the Atlantic coast to beyond the bend of the Niger.

It rose as Ghana (Wagadu) declined and trade moved south. Sundiata defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru around 1235, a story still told by griots in the Epic of Sundiata.

Its wealth came from the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure and from the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and copper. Its kings, the mansas, were Muslim, while most farmers kept older beliefs.

  • Mansa Musa (ruled about 1312 to 1337) brought the empire to its peak. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 made Mali's gold famous from Cairo to Europe.
  • Mali took Gao and Timbuktu, which became a centre of Islamic learning.
  • Ibn Battuta visited in 1352 and 1353 and praised the safety of its roads, while grumbling about the gifts he got.

After 1400 it weakened. Succession fights split the court, Tuareg raiders took Timbuktu in the 1430s, and the Songhai Empire took the eastern lands. Portuguese ships on the coast drew trade toward the Atlantic. By the 1600s Mali was a small Mandinka kingdom. The modern state of Mali took its name in 1960.
